nodes.name: Preparation of NiFe-LDH
nodes.procedure: NiFe-LDH was prepared via a gradient soaking process at room temperature to achieve good mechanical stability and a dense interlayer structure.
nodes.source_text: The first gradient soaking process was conducted according to the published literature to prepare NiFe-LDH with good mechanical stability... the cross-sectional SEM image further demonstrates that z-NiFe contains a dense interlayer

nodes.name: Zwitterion Modification
nodes.procedure: In the second gradient soaking process, zwitterions were added to obtain a secondary hierarchical structure. N1,N3-bis(carboxymethyl)-N1-(3-((carboxymethyl)dimethylammonio)propyl)-N1,N3,N3-trimethylpropane-1,3-diaminium (z-TCQ) was used as the zwitterion. The zwitterions were added to the NiFe-LDH at room temperature.

iR_correction.unit: stated in AEM-WE section for comparison

nodes.source_text: The electrocatalytic performance of z-NiFe for OER was evaluated in 1 M KOH using a three-electrode system... z-NiFe required a lower overpotential (178 mV) to achieve a current density of 100 mAcm-2... overpotential of z-NiFe was only 195 mV... Faradaic efficiency (FE) of z-NiFe during OER was close to 100%... anodic potential of z-NiFe remained stable over 12600 h... z-NiFe exhibited a more negative zeta potential (-23.64 mV)... KIE values are < 1.5.

In the AEM-WE device... the z-NiFe-catalyzed AEM-WE device delivers an industrially required hydrogen production current density of 1000 mA cm-2 at a cell voltage of 1.76 V... maintained stable operation for over 14000 h with a voltage degradation rate of 12.3 uV h-1. All the measurements were conducted in 1 M KOH without iR compensation.
When the temperature is raised to 80C, the z-NiFe-catalyzed AEM device exhibits high current density of 7860 mA cm-2 at a cell voltage of 2.00 V

nodes.characterization_summary: Secondary hierarchical structures of small nanosheets completely wrap the primary hierarchical structure, featuring a dense interlayer for mechanical stability.
nodes.evidence_snippet: SEM images of z-NiFe reveal that the secondary hierarchical structures ... completely wrap the primary hierarchical structure (Figures 1b and S2).

properties.description: Low and high magnification SEM images showing hierarchical micro-flower structures.

nodes.characterization_summary: z-NiFe exhibits a surface area of 238.36 m2g-1, higher than the 169.54 m2g-1 of NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: z-NiFe (238.36 m2g-1) exhibits a higher Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area compared to NiFe-LDH (169.54 m2g-1) (Figure S7).

nodes.characterization_summary: Identified as Ni2Fe(SO4)0.5(OH)6(H2O)3.85; z-NiFe shows a peak at 7.14° corresponding to an increased interlayer spacing of 1.23 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: z-NiFe exhibits a new diffraction peak at 7.14° , indicating a larger interlayer spacing (1.23 nm) than NiFe-LDH (1.07 nm) ... (Figure 1c).

nodes.characterization_summary: The Ni:Fe atomic ratio in z-NiFe is 1.25, lower than the 2.21 in NiFe-LDH; z-NiFe also shows suppressed metal dissolution during OER.
nodes.evidence_snippet: ICP-MS reveals that the atomic ratio of Ni:Fe in the z-NiFe is approximately 1.25, which is lower than that of NiFe-LDH (Ni:Fe ratio of 2.21).

nodes.characterization_summary: Observed carboxylate (1385, 1585 cm-1) and C-N+ (3012 cm-1) signals confirm zwitterion coordination to the metal centers.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The signal of C-N+ at 3012 cm-1 is present in both z-TCQ and z-NiFe... carboxylate groups (- COO-) at approximately 1385 and 1585 cm-1 (Figure S9).

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ Raman shows z-NiFe maintains a carbonate-rich (CO3 2-) alkaline microenvironment during OER, unlike NiFe-LDH which becomes acidic.
nodes.evidence_snippet: for z-NiFe, the peak area of CO3 2- consistently surpassed that of HCO3- with the voltage increase ... indicating an alkaline microenvironment (Figure 3a,b).

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe 2p and Ni 2p peaks show negative shifts in z-NiFe, indicating lower oxidation valence states due to zwitterion coordination.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XPS of the Fe 2p and Ni 2p peaks in z-NiFe further demonstrates lower oxidation valence states of Ni and Fe, as evidenced by negative shifts ... (Figure S10).

nodes.characterization_summary: Fe K-edge shift to lower energy confirms a reduced Fe valence state in z-NiFe.
nodes.evidence_snippet: XANES analysis reveals a slight shift of the Fe K-edge to lower energy in z-NiFe, indicating a reduced Fe valence state compared to NiFe-LDH (Figure 1e).

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM and TEM confirm honeycomb structures and interlayer lattice fringes consistent with the XRD-derived spacing.
nodes.evidence_snippet: HAADF-STEM) confirms that z-NiFe contains numerous honeycomb structures ... which is consistent with the TEM results (Figure S8).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping confirms the uniform distribution of C, N, O, Ni, and Fe elements within the honeycomb structures of z-NiFe.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping ... aligns with the distribution of elemental content (e.g., C, N, O, Ni, and Fe) observed in the TEM images (Figures S4-S6).

nodes.characterization_summary: z-NiFe exhibited a more negative zeta potential (-23.64 mV) compared to NiFe-LDH (-16.45 mV), indicating a higher local OH- concentration.
nodes.evidence_snippet: z-NiFe exhibited a more negative zeta potential (-23.64 mV) in 1 M KOH compared to NiFe-LDH (-16.45 mV).

nodes.characterization_summary: z-NiFe demonstrates significantly higher OH- conductivity and a faster OH- transfer rate than NiFe-LDH across various catalyst thicknesses.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 3c exhibits the OH- conductivity of z-NiFe as significantly higher than that of NiFe-LDH ... indicating that z-NiFe demonstrates a faster OH- transfer rate.

properties.observation: z-NiFe shows higher hydroxide conductivity compared to NiFe-LDH across the measured catalyst mass range.
